drafted_by: AI, requires clinician review before any real use.

questions.text: What is the main problem: dizziness, weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, vision changes, seizures, memory problems, or tremor?
questions.rationale: Clarifying the main neurological complaint guides the next branch of the interview.

questions.text: Did the symptoms come on suddenly, and when exactly did they begin?
questions.rationale: Abrupt onset with known time matters for stroke treatment windows.

questions.text: Have you had face drooping, arm or leg weakness, or slurred or confused speech?
questions.rationale: These are the cardinal signs of stroke.

questions.text: Have you lost vision in one or both eyes, or have double vision?
questions.rationale: Vision loss may signal stroke, optic nerve disease, or retinal artery occlusion.

questions.text: Is the dizziness a spinning feeling, or more like lightheadedness or being about to faint?
questions.rationale: True vertigo points to vestibular causes, while lightheadedness suggests cardiovascular causes.

questions.text: With the dizziness, do you have trouble walking, double vision, slurred speech, or severe headache?
questions.rationale: These features suggest posterior circulation stroke rather than benign vertigo.

questions.text: Did you lose consciousness or blank out? Did anyone see what happened?
questions.rationale: Witness account helps separate syncope from seizure.

questions.text: Did you have shaking, tongue biting, loss of bladder control, or confusion afterward?
questions.rationale: These features support a generalized seizure.

questions.text: Have you had seizures before, or are you on seizure medicine?
questions.rationale: History shapes whether this is a first seizure or breakthrough event.

questions.text: Do you have a new or severe headache with these symptoms?
questions.rationale: Headache with neurologic symptoms raises concern for bleeding or mass.

questions.text: Where is the numbness or tingling, and is it on one side, in a glove-stocking pattern, or in one limb?
questions.rationale: Distribution suggests central versus peripheral versus nerve root causes.

questions.text: Which muscles are weak, how fast did it develop, and is it getting worse?
questions.rationale: Pattern and tempo separate stroke, Guillain-Barre, myasthenia, and nerve compression.

questions.text: Have you had trouble with balance, walking, or falls?
questions.rationale: Gait disturbance can reflect cerebellar, vestibular, or myelopathic disease.

questions.text: Have you or others noticed memory loss, confusion, or personality changes?
questions.rationale: Acute confusion needs urgent evaluation, while gradual decline suggests dementia.

questions.text: Is the confusion new over hours or days, or fluctuating?
questions.rationale: Acute confusion suggests delirium, infection, stroke, or metabolic cause.

questions.text: Do you have tremor, stiffness, or slowed movement? Is the tremor at rest or with action?
questions.rationale: Tremor type helps separate Parkinson's disease from essential tremor.

questions.text: Do you have fever with neck stiffness or sensitivity to light?
questions.rationale: This suggests meningitis or encephalitis.

questions.text: Have you had a recent head injury? Do you take blood thinners?
questions.rationale: Trauma with anticoagulation raises risk of intracranial bleeding.

questions.text: Do you have new trouble controlling bladder or bowels, or numbness in the saddle area?
questions.rationale: These suggest spinal cord or cauda equina compression.

questions.text: Do you have high blood pressure, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, high cholesterol, or smoke?
questions.rationale: These are the major stroke risk factors.

questions.text: Have you started new medicines, or used alcohol, sedatives, or recreational drugs?
questions.rationale: Medications and substances commonly cause neurologic symptoms.

questions.text: How is your sleep and mood, and are you under unusual stress?
questions.rationale: Sleep deprivation and stress can lower seizure threshold and cause dizziness.

questions.text: Does anyone in your family have epilepsy, stroke, dementia, MS, or Parkinson's disease?
questions.rationale: Family history informs risk for hereditary neurologic disease.

questions.text: What is the main thing you are worried this could be?
questions.rationale: Understanding the patient's concern guides reassurance and follow-up questions.

red_flags.label: Face, arm, or speech symptoms
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report face drooping, arm or leg weakness, or slurred or confused speech?

red_flags.label: Sudden vision loss or double vision
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report sudden loss of vision or new double vision?

red_flags.label: Seizure or ongoing seizure activity
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient describe shaking, loss of consciousness, tongue biting, or postictal confusion?

red_flags.label: New acute confusion
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient or caregiver report confusion that is new over hours or days?

red_flags.label: Fever with stiff neck
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report fever with neck stiffness, light sensitivity, or severe headache?

red_flags.label: Head injury with deterioration
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report a recent head injury, especially on blood thinners, with worsening symptoms?

red_flags.label: Saddle numbness or bladder/bowel change
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient describe new loss of bladder or bowel control or numbness in the saddle area?

red_flags.label: Dizziness with brainstem features
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report dizziness with double vision, trouble walking, or slurred speech?
